polymer brush height and slip length depend on the shear rate and that the slip length of the glycocalyx decreases with increasing mean velocity.
the shear-induced flow of the polymer brush is governed by the screening of hydrodynamic interactions, while that of glycocalyx is governed by the bending rigidity.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the flow behaviour of two different systems, polymer brushes and glycocalyces, which are both present in nature.
the flow of fluids over polymer brushes and glycocalyces and the effects of shear on the structure of both systems.
the study of the effect of polymer grafting on surface slip and its implications on the transport of fluids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of a glycocalyx is not beneficial for the blood flow.
the glycocalyx is not a simple brush, but a more complicated structure, which, in addition to the polymer brush, contains a number of other elements such as proteoglycans, lipids and glycoproteins.
the slip length for the brush is independent of shear rate while that for the glycocalyx decreases with the shear rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the slip length for the glycocalyx is smaller than that for the polymer brush, and it is a function of the mean velocity, while the slip velocity of the polymer brush remains constant.
the presence of the polymer brush/glycocalyx layer on a surface can significantly alter the slip behaviour of the surface.
polymer brushes and glycocalyces, while similar in their structure, are different in their flow characteristics.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the case of the glycocalyx, the flow characteristics are determined by the bending of the fibres, while for polymer brushes the flow characteristics are dominated by the conformational entropy of the chains.
the slip length of a glycocalyx-covered surface is not constant but depends on the flow rate, which is a key parameter in blood rheology and haemodynamics.

, in the case of glycocalyx, a homogeneous shear flow does not accurately describe the actual flow field in microvessels, and that a more complex flow field is needed to describe the glycocalyx dynamics.
